questions.q: A file shows permissions -rwxr-x---. What can someone in the file's group do?
options: Read and execute it, but not write to it
questions.explain: The second triplet (group) is r-x: read and execute are set, write is not, so group members can read and run the file but not modify it.

questions.q: Which chmod command grants the owner full access, the group read and execute, and everyone else nothing?
questions.explain: 750 breaks down as owner=7 (rwx), group=5 (r-x), other=0 (---), matching rwxr-x---.

questions.q: What is the difference between chown and chgrp?
options: chown changes the owning user (and optionally group); chgrp changes only the owning group
chown changes permissions; chgrp changes ownership
They are two names for the exact same command with no difference
chgrp requires root but chown never does
questions.explain: chown can change the user, or user and group together with user:group syntax; chgrp changes only the group.

questions.q: With a umask of 022, what permissions does a newly created directory get?
questions.explain: Directories start at 777 by default. Subtracting the umask (022) gives 755 (rwxr-xr-x).

questions.q: Why do new regular files never get the execute bit, even with a very permissive umask like 000?
options: Because files start from a base of 666 (rw-rw-rw-), which has no execute bit to begin with
Because only root can create executable files
Because the umask always removes execute from files specifically
questions.explain: The umask only subtracts bits from the starting permissions. Files start at 666, which has no execute bit, so there's nothing for the umask to remove or leave in that position — it must be added explicitly with chmod.
